Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Data Scientist
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Affective Expression: Crying
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Vignette:
Juan's eyes still widened when he recalled the sound of sirens piercing through the night air. It was a sound that instantly transported him back to the endless nights spent in the hospital with his younger sister, Maria, who had been diagnosed with leukemia at just eight years old. Juan, then 15, had taken on a caretaking role, accompanying his parents to every doctor's appointment and sleepless night by Maria's bedside. The smell of antiseptic and sweat still lingered in his memory, evoking the same sense of dread he felt during those agonizing months. As Maria underwent treatment, Juan struggled to process his emotions, particularly anger and fear. He had come to believe that if he allowed himself to feel these emotions, he would lose control and be unable to support his family. So, he learned to suppress his anger, never expressing it, even when frustration simmered just below the surface. Similarly, he tried hard not to think about the trauma, pushing thoughts of Maria's illness deep into his mind. Years later, as a data scientist, Juan found himself avoiding medical settings at all costs. The mere sight of an ambulance or hospital building would send his heart racing, and he would quickly change direction to avoid passing by. He couldn't bear the thought of being in a physical examination room again, reliving the memories of Maria's frail body undergoing test after test. But avoidance only seemed to heighten Juan's sense of threat. Ordinary sounds – a car horn, a sudden knock on the door – would startle him, making him jump with a physical reactivity that left his heart pounding in his chest. He began to have difficulty falling asleep, feeling an overwhelming need to stay alert and vigilant, as if danger lurked around every corner. Memories of Maria's illness remained fragmented and disjointed in Juan's mind. He couldn't put the sequence of events in order, recalling moments out of context – the sound of beeping machines, his mother's tears, Maria's pale face. It was as if his brain had jumbled up the narrative to protect him from the full force of the trauma. When memories did surface, they felt unreal, like a nightmare that he couldn't shake. Recalling specific moments still filled Juan with terror – the night Maria's fever spiked, or the day she received her diagnosis. His mind would relive those moments in vivid detail, leaving him shaken and gasping for air. He began to wonder if he'd ever be able to escape the grip of these memories. As time passed, Juan's avoidance behaviors started to impact his daily life. He found himself skipping social gatherings or canceling plans with friends if they involved going near a hospital or medical facility. His relationships suffered as a result, and he felt increasingly isolated. It was when his manager at work expressed concern about his declining performance that Juan finally realized he needed help. The constant hypervigilance had taken a toll on his concentration, and the memories of Maria's illness continued to haunt him. He began to fear that if he didn't confront these demons, they would consume him entirely. Juan sought therapy with a mix of trepidation and hope. He hoped that by facing his trauma head-on, he might finally find some peace and learn to live with the memories of his sister's illness without being controlled by them. The thought of confronting those sirens, both literal and metaphorical, still filled him with dread, but he knew it was a necessary step towards healing.
